what_it_does: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a technique for rendering photorealistic 3D scenes in real time: instead of triangles, the scene is represented as millions of small translucent blobs (Gaussians), each with a position, shape, color, and opacity, and the image is formed by projecting and blending them onto the screen. This is far more computationally demanding than traditional rendering, making it impractical on the chips inside smartphones and tablets (mobile SoCs — System-on-Chip processors). Lumina attacks this with two observations: most of the blobs in a scene do not change meaningfully from one video frame to the next (temporal coherence), so their contributions can be cached and skipped rather than recomputed; and the accumulated color values from groups of blobs can be stored (radiance caching) so that only the changed portions need to be re-blended. A dedicated hardware accelerator called LuminCore is built alongside these algorithmic ideas to make the cache lookups and partial updates efficient, enabling real-time 3DGS rendering within the power budget of a mobile device.
